title: Honor of the humble
hook: the Ardas names God by what God is to those with nothing: honor of the dishonored, strength of the weak, shelter of the shelterless

segments.voice: Yesterday: vichhora, and your line: doors left behind. Today the Ardas turns from places to people, the ones nobody notices.

Every school has the kid who eats lunch alone. Every office has the person whose name nobody quite remembers. Every family has the cousin who's always in the kitchen while the photos are being taken. People often reach for big titles when they address God: king, judge, almighty. Near its end, the Ardas also does something quieter. Just before the one praying turns to their own request, it names God by who God is for exactly those people. The kid at the empty table. The one in the kitchen.
screen: `THE KID WHO EATS ALONE.` → `BIG TITLES FOR GOD.` → `THE ARDAS CHOOSES QUIETER NAMES.`

segments.voice: The line runs: nimaaniaan de maan, nitaaniaan de taan, niotiaan di ot, sache pita Waheguru. Honor of the dishonored, strength of the weak, shelter of the shelterless, true Father, Waheguru. Look at how it's built. Maan is honor, dignity, standing. Taan is strength. Ot is shelter, something to lean on. Put ni- in front of each and you get the people who lack it: the nimaana, with no standing; the nitaana, with no strength; the niota, with no one to lean on. So the Ardas doesn't describe God floating far above. It describes God as the very thing each of them is missing. No honor? God is your honor. No strength? God is your strength. This isn't new to the prayer. Guru Nanak said it in his own hymns. In Sri Rag, on ang 15, he says Nanak stands with the lowest of the low, and has no wish to copy the great; and where the lowly are cared for, there the Lord's glance of grace falls. Sikh life tried to make that physical. In langar, everyone sits on the same floor and eats the same food, whatever their caste or their bank balance. In the Ardas, the rich donor and the person who came in for a free meal say these words together, standing side by side. So the line works two ways. It's comfort for anyone who feels small today. And it's a quiet question for anyone who doesn't: if God's honor is with the overlooked, where should mine be?
screen: `MAAN, TAAN, OT: HONOR, STRENGTH, SHELTER.` · `NI-: THE ONES WHO LACK IT.` · `GURU NANAK STANDS WITH THE LOWLY.` · `LANGAR PUTS IT ON THE FLOOR.` · then, large: `STRENGTH OF THE WEAK.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person who gets overlooked, at work, at school, maybe in your own family, and see their face. Notice what they might be missing today, standing, strength, or someone to lean on, and simply hold them in your attention, the way the Ardas holds them. If you pray, say the three words softly: maan, taan, ot.
Maan, honor, dignity, standing: the Ardas names God as the honor of those with none, the strength of the weak, the shelter of the shelterless, maan, taan, ot.
Your line: strength of the weak. Honor, strength and shelter, for those who have none. That's day six hundred thirty-two.

howItsDone: Near the end of the Ardas, Sikhs address God as nimaaniaan de maan, nitaaniaan de taan, niotiaan di ot, the honor, strength and shelter of those without them, just before the specific request of the day.

original.note: Gurmukhi: honor, dignity, standing; a nimaana is someone without it.

trapdoor: what you thought: a polite list of God's titles.
what it means: God named as the very thing each overlooked person is missing: honor, strength, shelter.
what a scholar hears: each word is built as a pair, maan and nimaana, taan and nitaana, ot and niota, echoing Guru Nanak's own hymns about standing with the lowly.

chat.says: That line in the Ardas about honor and strength: whose honor is it talking about?
options: Those with none: God is the honor, strength and shelter of people who lack them.
The Gurus and martyrs: it honors the famous Sikhs the Ardas named earlier on.
The donors: it thanks those whose giving keeps the gurdwara and langar going.
chat.meaning: Nimaaniaan de maan, nitaaniaan de taan, niotiaan di ot: God is honor, strength and shelter for those who lack them.

nimaana.meaning: one with no honor or standing
